Choose a sound

Every analysis automatically saves a recording and a JSON report in P:\Marju\chunktest, plus a blueprint and matching sound file in P:\Marju\commands\blueprints. Local computer only. This does not teach or change any commands.

Type 2 labels Stable regions longer than 7.5% of the recording as Noise chunks (white, N1/N2…). These are not regular chunks or Between chunks, and have no individual Play button. Exactly 7.5% is kept as Stable. “Noise” is an experimental label, not proof of background noise. The full sound and waveform are preserved.

Example: 0.1 treats every sample from −0.1 to +0.1 as zero before the Type 2 amplitude envelope is calculated. Range: 0–1. Samples are not removed from time. The original recording, raw waveform and Fourier spectra stay unchanged. Set 0 to turn this filter off. Changing the value reanalyzes when you leave the box or press Enter.

Type 2 uses Math.abs(sample), a positive amplitude envelope, and the types Raising, Going down and Stable. Sensitive uses 30 ms averaging/smoothing and a 1% change threshold; changes shorter than 40 ms are merged. Very sensitive can also pick up more noise. Type 1 is unchanged. Switching settings reanalyzes and saves the current sound without recording again.

Chunk analysis

The pitch graph and chunks will appear here.

1. Raw sound waveform

The decoded samples, converted to mono at 16 kHz, with no pitch smoothing. Each screen column shows its minimum and maximum sample amplitude. Play the sound: the red marker follows playback. Shading shows the existing pitch chunks.

Playback position: 0 ms

2. Fourier transform — full recording

Which frequencies are strongest? This graph averages the power of short, overlapping FFT windows across the recording. It shows frequency strength, not when each frequency occurred. The separate time strip below the spectrum has a red playback marker; the spectrum itself remains a recording average.

Analyze a sound to see its frequencies.

3. Fourier transform — chunks and gaps

Listen to the original audio from the exact time range shown in this region’s Fourier graph.

Analyze a sound to inspect its regions.

The red marker follows the recording. Green shading marks between-chunks regions; the dark outline marks the selected region. FFT: 2,048 samples per Hann window (128 ms), 20 ms hop, 7.8125 Hz bins. Levels are relative to digital full scale, not physical loudness. Short regions are zero-padded; padding does not add frequency detail. Frequencies above 8 kHz are not retained by the 16 kHz analysis audio. The Mel spectrogram below shows the next step.

4. Mel spectrogram — sound colours over time

Time goes left to right. Mel frequency bands go from low at the bottom to high at the top. Colour shows each band’s strength. The same chunk boundaries are drawn on top; the red line follows playback. This is a sound measurement, not word recognition. The MFCC graph below compresses these Mel measurements into sound-shape features.

Analyze a recording to see its Mel bands over time.

5. MFCCs — sound shape over time

Each time frame is compressed into sound-shape coefficients. C1–C12 are shown here; their numbers are not frequencies. The red line follows playback.

Analyze a sound to see its MFCCs.

6. Sound fingerprint — an experimental feature vector

The recording fingerprint excludes Noise, Between chunks and Closed chunks. Selected regions are measured inside their exact boundaries, with final windows zero-padded. C0 is excluded to reduce volume influence, but recordings can still differ with microphones, speakers, noise and volume. Very short chunks give limited information.

Analyze a recording to build a fingerprint.

Type 1 — pitch trace and boundaries

Bright green regions marked B1, B2…: Between chunks. These can contain sound or silence. Pitch chunks: teal rising · amber falling · blue stable. Dark line: smoothed pitch. Faint line: raw pitch. Gray area below: sound energy. Blank pitch means no reliable voiced pitch, not necessarily silence.

Compare chunk patterns

Analyze one sound and keep it as the reference. Then analyze another sound: compare the number of chunks first, their types in order second, and relative pitch ranks third. Exact Hz and exact lengths are not compared. This test does not change command recognition.

No reference selected. The reference stays only until this page is refreshed.

Pitch rank 1 is lowest. Equal pitch levels rounded to 0.1 Hz share a rank. No reliable pitch means no pitch rank. Length rank is shown separately but is not used in this comparison.
